The Zombie Apocalypse: A Population Dynamics Problem

For the next several lessons, we are going to dive into linear algebra. We are taking a break from calculus for a while, and in fact, today we aren’t even going to look at the matrices or vectors that you might typically associate with linear algebra. If you have never seen linear algebra before, or if it has been a long time and you have forgotten the details, do not worry. We are building the intuition from the ground up.

To do that, we are starting with a simple, yet highly realistic scenario: a zombie apocalypse. (This specific flavor of zombie linear algebra is inspired by a great YouTube video by Zach Star, with a little bit of The Cranberries and Michael Jackson thrown in for good measure).

Imagine a closed system where we start with a small group of survivors. At hour zero, everyone is human. Let’s say we have 15 humans and 0 zombies.

Every hour, the zombies attack, and 20\% of the human population turns into zombies. Fortunately, our nanoscience lab has developed an aerosolized cure! But it is not a permanent fix. Every hour, the cure manages to turn 10\% of the zombie population back into humans.

Before we do any math, what does your intuition tell you will happen after a long time? When I asked this in class, many of you guessed that the zombies would eventually overrun the humans and win. It makes sense—the infection rate (20\%) is double the cure rate (10\%). But as we will see, population dynamics can be surprising. We actually reach a stable equilibrium! Let’s break down exactly how we get there.

Tracking the Horde: Hour by Hour

To understand the long-term behavior, we need to track the populations step-by-step. Let’s define some variables so we can keep our bookkeeping organized:

  • n: The current time step, measured in hours (an integer: 0, 1, 2, \dots).

  • h_n: The number of humans at the n^{\text{th}} hour.

  • z_n: The number of zombies at the n^{\text{th}} hour.

Hour 0 to Hour 1

At the very beginning (Hour 0), our initial state is: \begin{align} h_0 &= 15 \tag{1}\\ z_0 &= 0 \tag{2} \end{align} The total population is h_0 + z_0 = 15.

Now, let’s step forward to Hour 1. What happens to the humans? They lose 20\% of their population to the zombie horde, which means 80\% of them stay human. Meanwhile, they gain 10\% of whatever the zombie population was. \begin{align} h_1 &= (\text{Humans who stay human}) + (\text{Zombies who get cured}) \nonumber \\ h_1 &= 0.8(h_0) + 0.1(z_0) \nonumber \\ h_1 &= 0.8(15) + 0.1(0) = 12 \tag{3} \end{align}

What about the zombies? They gain the 20\% of humans who were infected, and they keep 90\% of their own population (since 10\% were cured). \begin{align} z_1 &= (\text{Humans who turn}) + (\text{Zombies who stay zombies}) \nonumber \\ z_1 &= 0.2(h_0) + 0.9(z_0) \nonumber \\ z_1 &= 0.2(15) + 0.9(0) = 3 \tag{4} \end{align}

At Hour 1, we have 12 humans and 3 zombies. Notice that 12 + 3 = 15. The total population is conserved. Nobody is born, nobody dies, and nobody leaves the island.

Hour 1 to Hour 2

Let’s do one more step by hand to make sure we see the mechanics. To find the populations at Hour 2, we apply the exact same rates, but this time we use the populations from Hour 1 (h_1 = 12, z_1 = 3) as our starting point.

For the humans at Hour 2: \begin{align} h_2 &= 0.8(h_1) + 0.1(z_1) \nonumber \\ h_2 &= 0.8(12) + 0.1(3) \nonumber \\ h_2 &= 9.6 + 0.3 = 9.9 \tag{5} \end{align}

For the zombies at Hour 2: \begin{align} z_2 &= 0.2(h_1) + 0.9(z_1) \nonumber \\ z_2 &= 0.2(12) + 0.9(3) \nonumber \\ z_2 &= 2.4 + 2.7 = 5.1 \tag{6} \end{align}

At Hour 2, we have 9.9 humans and 5.1 zombies. (Yes, fractional humans and zombies are a bit gruesome to picture, but remember this is a mathematical model representing statistical averages!). Once again, check the total: 9.9 + 5.1 = 15. The conservation holds.

Let’s do a quick check of your skills. Calculate the number of zombies at Hour 3 using the populations from Hour 2 (h_2 = 9.9, z_2 = 5.1).

To find z_3, we take 20\% of the human population from Hour 2 and add it to 90\% of the zombie population from Hour 2. That gives us 0.2(9.9) + 0.9(5.1) = 1.98 + 4.59 = 6.57 zombies. The horde is growing!

Building the Mathematical Model

We just calculated Hour 1 and Hour 2. No one in class wanted to calculate Hour 3 by hand, and understandably so. To avoid doing endless arithmetic, we need to be smart about modeling the populations. We need to identify the pattern and write a generalized system of equations that applies at every time step.

If we want to know the population at any hour n, we just look at the population one step prior, at hour n-1. The coefficients (the conversion rates) never change.

This gives us our formal mathematical model—a system of linear difference equations: \begin{equation} \begin{cases} h_n = 0.8 h_{n-1} + 0.1 z_{n-1} \\ z_n = 0.2 h_{n-1} + 0.9 z_{n-1} \end{cases} \tag{7} \end{equation}

Notice what happens if we add these two equations together: \begin{align} h_n + z_n &= (0.8 h_{n-1} + 0.1 z_{n-1}) + (0.2 h_{n-1} + 0.9 z_{n-1}) \nonumber \\ h_n + z_n &= (0.8 + 0.2)h_{n-1} + (0.1 + 0.9)z_{n-1} \nonumber \\ h_n + z_n &= 1 h_{n-1} + 1 z_{n-1} \tag{8} \end{align} This is the mathematical proof of our conservation rule. Whatever the humans lose, the zombies gain, and vice versa. The total population is strictly conserved at every step.

Letting the Machine Do the Work

As a human, your job is to understand the concepts and the meaning behind the math. Repetitive, iterative calculations are best left for machines.

We can use Excel to have the computer do the math for us, repeatedly and instantly. Since not everyone was familiar with Excel, we walked through the setup carefully in class.

The trick to making a good spreadsheet model is separating your constants (the conversion rates) from your variables (the populations at each hour). We put the rates in a block at the top left, and build our timeline on the right.

When we program the population evolution, we need to tell Excel to always look at the same rate cells, even as we drag the formula down to calculate later hours. We do this using absolute references, denoted by the dollar sign ($).

For example, if our rate for "zombies from humans" (0.2) is in cell A5, and the previous hour’s human population is in E2, we write $A$5 * E2. The dollar signs lock both the column and the row. When you drag the formula down to row 3, E2 will automatically update to E3 (relative reference), but $A$5 will stay exactly where it is.

Why is it important to use relative references (like E2) for the previous hour’s population, rather than locking them with dollar signs?

We want the population reference to slide down row by row as we calculate future hours. If we locked the population cell with dollar signs, Excel would just keep calculating Hour 1 over and over again instead of moving forward in time.

Population Equilibrium

Once our formulas are set up, we can drag them down to Hour 50 and plot the results. Let’s look at what actually happens to our survivors.

The populations don’t just keep swinging wildly, and the zombies don’t consume everyone. The curves flatten out. We reach a population equilibrium! After a long time, the system stabilizes at exactly 5 humans and 10 zombies.

Why does this happen? Equilibrium is reached when the number of humans turning into zombies is exactly balanced by the number of zombies being cured. In mathematical terms, the net flow is zero: \begin{align} 0.2(h_{\text{eq}}) &= 0.1(z_{\text{eq}}) \nonumber \\ \frac{z_{\text{eq}}}{h_{\text{eq}}} &= \frac{0.2}{0.1} = 2 \tag{9} \end{align}

The final equilibrium ratio is determined entirely by the ratio of the conversion rates. Because the infection rate (20\%) is twice as fast as the cure rate (10\%), the equilibrium state will always have twice as many zombies as humans. Since our total population is conserved at 15, the only way to have a 2-to-1 ratio is to have 10 zombies and 5 humans.

If the rates were different—say, 50\% of humans turn into zombies, but only 5\% of zombies are cured—the ratio would be 10-to-1, and the humans would be in much worse shape.

Given this new 10-to-1 zombie-to-human ratio, and keeping our total population conserved at 15, exactly how many humans and zombies are left at this new equilibrium?

If the ratio is 10 zombies for every 1 human, we can think of the population as being divided into 11 equal parts. Since the total population is 15, we have 15/11 \approx 1.36 humans and 150/11 \approx 13.64 zombies. The humans are definitely losing this battle!

This idea of tracking states as they evolve through constant transition rates is the bedrock of linear algebra. Next time, we will take this exact same system and learn how to write it using vectors and matrices, which will unlock a whole new set of tools for analyzing complex systems.
